newsitem.title: CHINA: China Grains-Corn imports possible next year.
newsitem.headline: China Grains-Corn imports possible next year.

text.p: China is unlikely to import corn this year despite the high probability of a shrunken crop but may have to turn to imports at the end of 1998, grains traders said on Thursday.
Government corn stocks were sufficient to support the market at least until the end of next year, grain traders said, although it was too early to tell what China's corn output would be.
"China will not import corn now, but I don't know about the end of next year," said a senior trader.
It could be that certain joint venture feed mills turned to corn imports in around six or seven months, another trader said.
He said the price of imported corn would be roughly 1,200 yuan (US$144) to 1,300 yuan, C&F China.
Bumper corn harvests over the past two years, yielding a total of over 200 million tonnes, had left warehouses full of surplus corn to fill in any gaps from this year's lean harvest, sources said.
"By about March 1998 there will be a clearer picture of the government's policy towards corn imports," said one trader.
For the time being, although corn prices were rising and the harvest would almost certainly drop, the government was reluctant to import for fear of hurting incentives to plant, traders said.

"Corn prices are going up, but they have been very low for over a year," another trader noted. Corn prices in Dalian continued their march upwards on Thursday, with prices heard as high as 1,150 yuan per tonne, FOB Dalian, compared to 1,140 yuan per tonne on Tuesday and 1,060 yuan per tonne earlier this month.

"The Grain Bureau has adjusted its price upwards to 1,150 yuan per tonne," said one China-based grains trader, noting that the government currently held about 90 percent of the corn stocks. This figure could not be confirmed. "The price advancement is mainly due to fears of a drought impact," he said.
Another trader said that corn supplies from the north of China to the south had been held up by rainy weather at southern ports which made discharging cargoes difficult.

"Feed mills in the south only have supplies for a week or 10 days, so end-users are nervous about supplies and ordering more from the north," said one grains source, noting this had contributed to the price jump.
Others said that overall, a reduced planted acreage and farmers' reluctance to invest in fertilisers and irrigation due to poor returns had a significant, if not greater, impact.
On Dalian's futures' exchange, punters favoured long positions, one grains trader said.
"I don't think there is a single short position there," he said. (US$1=8.3 yuan)
